about.title: About Orbisol
about.what: Orbisol helps farmers explore crop rotation strategies using NASA Earth observations, local soil information, crop characteristics and their own priorities.

origin.static: Built-in data for the demo region

season.hotThreshold: Hot day here means above {{t}} °C: the hottest 10% of these days in {{bFrom}}–{{bTo}}.

hotDays.name: Hot days
hotDays.what: Days hotter than usual for this time of year. Many hot days can stress crops and raise water use.

rainTotal.name: Rain
rainTotal.what: Total rain that fell in this window.

heavyRainDays.name: Extreme rain days
heavyRainDays.what: Days with 20 mm of rain or more. These can flood fields, wash away soil and damage crops.

frostDays.name: Frost days
frostDays.what: Nights when the air 2 m above ground fell below 0 °C.

soilWetness.name: Soil moisture (top layer)
soilWetness.what: How much of the space in the top few centimetres of soil holds water: 0% is bone dry, 100% is soaked. From a NASA model that does not include canal irrigation, so irrigated fields are wetter than shown.

waterBalance.name: Water balance
waterBalance.what: Rain minus evaporation demand. Below zero means the air took more water than rain gave; canal water or stored soil water had to fill the gap.

greenness.name: Greenness (NDVI)
greenness.what: How green and leafy plants look from space. Low greenness can mean stress, bare soil or harvest.

et0Total.name: Evaporation demand (ET0)
et0Total.what: How much water a healthy, well-watered grass field would lose to the air (FAO-56 calls it reference evapotranspiration, ET0). Hot, dry, windy, sunny days raise it. Most crops need about this much water or more.

season.gap: Data gap: satellite greenness is not loaded yet for this field.
season.frostFlag: ground frost can happen even when the air stays just above 0 °C
season.rainFlag: canal water is not in these numbers; your canal turn matters more than rain here
season.sure1: Weather numbers come from NASA POWER, a model that works in squares about 50 km wide. They describe your area, not your exact field, and they do not include canal irrigation.
season.sure2: Normal is the middle value (median) of the same days in {{n}} past years. The usual range covers the middle 80% of those years.
season.sure3: Above or below normal means this window was in the top or bottom third of those years.
season.coverage: Days with data in this window: {{pct}}%.
season.sure4: Evaporation demand from this model may read higher than at a local weather station in canal-irrigated areas, because the model does not see the cooler, more humid air over irrigated fields. Compare it with normal rather than reading it as an exact amount.

green.window: {{from}} to {{to}} ({{n}} satellite images, one every 16 days) vs the same days in 2001–2020.
green.method: Middle value of farmland pixels (250 m squares) within {{km}} km of your pin (NASA MODIS land cover); cloudy or poor-quality pixels are left out.
green.gapOutside: Data gap: satellite greenness is precomputed only for the demo region in this version.
green.scale: NDVI runs from about 0 (bare soil, buildings) to about 0.9 (dense green crops).

imerg.note: Measured from space by NASA GPM IMERG for a 10 km cell; normal = same days {{from}}–{{to}} ({{n}} years). Model rain above and satellite rain here can differ.

season.rangeAria: This season {{value}}; normal {{normal}}; usual range {{lo}} to {{hi}}.

why.existing: This is your current rotation: the starting point the others are compared with.
why.betterFor: Scores better than your current rotation on "{{priority}}", one of your priorities.
why.balanced: A balanced option for your priorities; it does not beat your current rotation on any single one.

evidence.waterNeed: {{crop}} needs about {{mm}} mm of water over its season (range {{low}}–{{high}} mm): FAO-56 crop factor × evaporation demand at your field.
evidence.et0Source: Evaporation demand (ET0) is the 1991–2020 daily average from NASA POWER weather data at your field.
evidence.bareDays: Field bare about {{days}} days a year, {{hot}} of them in the hottest months.
evidence.legume: {{crop}} is a legume: it adds nitrogen to the soil.

benefit.lessWater: About {{pct}}% less crop water need than your current rotation.
benefit.moreCover: Field covered about {{days}} more days a year: less bare soil for wind and water to erode.
benefit.lessBareInHeat: {{days}} fewer bare days in the hottest months.
benefit.nitrogen: {{crop}} adds nitrogen to the soil (legume), which can help the next crop.
benefit.pestBreak: Brings in a new plant family ({{families}}). A different host can interrupt pests and diseases that live on one family.

gap.market: Market prices and demand are not in Orbisol. Check local buyers before switching.
gap.varieties: Variety choice and seed availability are not included.
gap.proxyStages: {{crop}} growth stages borrow FAO-56 values from a similar crop.
gap.forage: Fodder value of {{crop}} residues is not counted (no source found).
gap.sowingSource: {{crop}} sowing dates come from a general source; check with your local agriculture office.
gap.irrigationModel: Weather data comes from a NASA model that does not see canal irrigation.

risk.saltSensitive: {{crop}} is $t(saltRating.{{rating}}) to salt: yield starts to fall when soil salt is above {{ece}} dS/m (ECe, a lab measure of soil salt). You said your soil is salty.

vulnerable.hot: {{crop}} is in a sensitive stage during the hottest months ({{months}}).
vulnerable.frost: {{crop}} is in a sensitive stage in frost-prone months ({{months}}).
vulnerable.heavyRain: {{crop}} is in a sensitive stage when heavy rain is most frequent ({{months}}).

risk.overlap: Crops overlap by {{days}} days: the next crop must be sown into the standing one before its harvest (relay sowing), or later than shown.
risk.moreWater: Needs about {{pct}}% more water than your current rotation.
risk.moreBare: Field is bare {{days}} more days a year ({{hot}} bare days in the hottest months): more erosion and weeds.
risk.newCrop: {{crop}} is new to this rotation: seed, skills, machinery and buyers need checking.
risk.tightTurnaround: Less than a week between the previous harvest and sowing {{crop}}.

terrain.title: Slope and erosion
terrain.slope: FAO slope class {{code}}: {{name}} (SRTM, about 270 m cells within 1 km).
terrain.waterLow: On land this flat, rain water runs off slowly: water erosion from slope is low. Levelling and bunds still matter in heavy rain.
terrain.waterHigher: Sloping land: heavy rain can wash soil away. Cover crops and bunds help.
terrain.noise: Very local (30 m) satellite slopes are mostly noise on flat plains, so the wider value is used.
terrain.bareWindy: Your field is bare about {{days}} days in the windiest months: dry bare soil can blow away. Covering it in that window helps.

waterFit.title: Water fit with your canal turn
waterFit.noCanal: Orbisol then checks, month by month, whether water comes often enough for each crop.
waterFit.summaryOver: Your turn every {{days}} days is longer than the crop can safely wait in: {{months}}.
waterFit.summaryOk: Your turn every {{days}} days fits every month we could check.
waterFit.intro: Safe interval = how many days the soil around the roots can keep the crop supplied before it starts to suffer (FAO-56: easily usable soil water ÷ crop water use per day).
waterFit.soilAssumed: Soil not set: using loam. Set your soil in My farm for a better answer.
waterFit.youngNote: Young crop: roots are not deep yet, so the real safe interval is shorter than shown. Too-long turns are still flagged; a fit is not confirmed.
waterFit.limitVolume: Limitation: we do not know how much water your canal turn brings (flow and hours vary), so we assume each turn fills the soil around the roots. If a turn does not fill the field, the safe interval is shorter.
waterFit.limitRain: Rain is not counted, so monsoon months may be easier than shown.
waterFit.sources: From FAO-56 Table 19 (soil water), Table 22 (root depth and p, smaller depth as advised for irrigation scheduling, p adjusted for crop water use) and crop water use = FAO-56 Kc × NASA POWER ET0.
waterFit.empty: Add your canal turn in My farm to see this.

trend.title: Long-term trend, {{from}}–{{to}}
trend.notForecast: Observed trend, not a forecast. It shows how past years changed, not what next year will bring.
trend.tooShort: Not enough complete years for a trend.

hotDays.name: Hot days per year
hotDays.what: Days with a maximum above {{t}} °C (the hottest 10% of days in 1991–2020 here).
hotDays.decades: First 10 years: about {{a}} hot days a year. Last 10 years: about {{b}}.
hotDays.chart: Hot days per year, one point per year, with the trend line
hotDays.up: Hot days have become more common.
hotDays.down: Hot days have become less common here.
hotDays.unclear: No clear change: the year-to-year swing is bigger than the trend.

trend.legend: Solid line: each year. Dashed line: straight-line trend.
trend.caveat: from a NASA model that averages over squares about 50 km wide, not a local station; model trends can shift when the satellite and station data fed into it change, and this has not been checked against a local station
trend.method: Complete calendar years only. Change per decade = best-fit straight line × 10 years; the likely range (95%) shows how sure that is. If the range crosses zero, the change is called unclear.
trend.irrigation: Irrigated areas can cool daytime extremes (watered fields evaporate and cool the air), and this NASA model averages over a square about 50 km wide, so it mixes your area with its surroundings.

warmNights.name: Warm nights per year
warmNights.what: Nights with a minimum above {{t}} °C (the warmest 10% of nights in 1991–2020 here). Warm nights stress crops and animals because they do not cool down.
warmNights.decades: First 10 years: about {{a}} warm nights a year. Last 10 years: about {{b}}.
warmNights.chart: Warm nights per year, one point per year, with the trend line
warmNights.up: Warm nights have become more common.
warmNights.down: Warm nights have become less common here.
warmNights.unclear: No clear change: the year-to-year swing is bigger than the trend.

txx.name: Hottest day of the year
txx.what: The highest daily maximum in each year.
txx.decades: First 10 years: about {{a}} °C on average. Last 10 years: about {{b}} °C.
txx.chart: Hottest day of each year in °C, one point per year, with the trend line
txx.up: The hottest day of the year has become hotter.
txx.down: The hottest day of the year has become a little cooler here.
txx.unclear: No clear change: the year-to-year swing is bigger than the trend.

waterBalance.name: Rain minus evaporation demand (ET0) per year
waterBalance.what: Below zero means the air took more water than rain gave; canal water had to fill the gap.
waterBalance.decades: First 10 years: about {{a}} mm a year. Last 10 years: about {{b}} mm.
waterBalance.chart: Yearly rain minus ET0 in mm, one point per year, with the trend line
waterBalance.up: The yearly gap has become smaller (wetter balance): more rain and lower evaporation demand.
waterBalance.down: The yearly gap has grown (drier balance).
waterBalance.unclear: No clear change: the year-to-year swing is bigger than the trend.

heat2050.title: Hot days around {{from}}–{{to}}
heat2050.notForecast: Climate model projection, not a forecast. It shows what climate models give for a 20-year period if world greenhouse-gas emissions follow one path, not the weather in any year.
heat2050.what: Days a year with a maximum above {{t}} °C (the same line as the observed trend), from {{n}} climate models for this 25 km square. Shown as a range across models.
heat2050.ssp245: If world emissions follow a middle path (SSP2-4.5)
heat2050.counts: Models give {{base}} hot days a year in {{bFrom}}–{{bTo}} and {{fut}} around 2050.
heat2050.bias: these models run cooler than the NASA POWER grid here (about 36 hot days a year observed in 1995–2014), so trust the change more than the counts
heat2050.scenarios: Change = 2041–2060 average minus the same model's 1995–2014 average. SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5 are the IPCC's names for a middle and a high emissions path; which one the world follows is not known.

timeline.ndviCaption: What NASA's MODIS satellite sees on your field
timeline.ndviHint: Greenness (NDVI) in a usual year, 2001–2020: the middle value of farmland within 3 km of your pin. Higher = greener, leafier crops; low = bare soil or harvest.

ndvi.plain: A number satellites get from how much red and near-infrared light plants reflect. About 0 means bare soil or water, 0.2 to 0.3 thin or dry plants, 0.6 and above dense green crops. It rises as a crop grows and drops after harvest.

et0.plain: How thirsty the air is: the water a short, well-watered grass field would lose to the air, in mm. Heat, sun, wind and dry air raise it. A crop's water need is about ET0 times a crop factor (FAO-56).

waterBalance.plain: Rain minus evaporation demand over the same days. A number below zero is the gap that canal water or water stored in the soil had to fill. Here it is below zero for most of the year.

soilAnomaly.plain: How much wetter or drier the top soil is than normal for these days of the year: this season's value against the usual range. The NASA model behind it does not see canal water, so irrigated fields are wetter than shown.

frost.plain: Frost is when the air near the ground falls to 0 °C or below; it can burn leaves and flowers. A month is marked as frost risk when, in 1991 to 2020, it had a frost night at least once every two years on average.
